About three months ago I started going to see a therapist. I had been suffering from anxiety and depression for a really long time, and I had been suffering in silence. The first day of therapy I realized this was something that I had been needing for a long time. It wasn't until our third or fourth session that more memories started coming to the surface. These memories had been repressed for quite some time and I finally felt like I had somebody to talk to about them to. I didn't feel any judgement, there was no eye roll or glaring. There was no, "that was a long time ago, get over it". I was able to just speak the words as they came to me.

Around three months ago I started seeing a therapist for mental health reasons. Specifically it was Anxiety and Depression that was bothering me. I had felt sad and sick for a couple of days so decided it was time to change my life. The therapist was a 4 hour drive away - nothing for me, as I had a Ducati Supersport bike. After 4 sessions, I was starting to get somewhere. I told the therapist everything and I felt like I could tell them my life story. They weren't judgemental and after the fourth session, they said that I was healed and that I would probably never need a therapist again. I was really happy with that result and thought that was money well spent, especially to cure it so fast.

My father has been ill for a few weeks now and it's been getting our whole family down.  My mom hasn't said anything, but I know she's worried sick about how she is going to be able to pay the bills while my dad is out of work.  It's been a dark cloud over the house.  Today things changed!  I was finally offered a promotion at my job!  This means I will be able to help them out for a change.  My dad has always supported me and now it's my opportunity to return the favor.  It feels so good to be recognized for all the hard work I've put in at my company.  I think this is going to be a great start of a new beginning.  My dad looked so proud when I told him about the promotion.

For several weeks now, my father's illness has cast a heavy shadow over our entire household. While my mother tries to stay strong and silent, the stress over our mounting bills and my dad's lost income is written all over her face. It has been an incredibly draining time for everyone. However, the atmosphere finally shifted today because I was officially offered a promotion at work. This advancement provides the financial stability I need to step up and support my parents during this crisis. My father has spent his whole life providing for me, and being able to return that favor is a massive relief. After months of putting in extra hours, it feels genuinely validating to be recognized by my manager. Seeing the genuine look of pride in my dad's eyes when I shared the news gave me hope that we are finally turning a corner.

I`m not sure what I expected of my new home but I thought it would have been more organised than my last country. Overall I am glad it is all resolved.

The story I am writing about is a medical story. For my whole life, I have had a fainting disorder. My doctor thought it might be a condition called POTS. It took months to get a cardiologist to order the test, for some reason. They seemed to test me for everything else first. I eventually went to a heart hospital and had a test called a tilt table test. In this test they strap you to a table, with a pillow behind your head. You lie down for a while, and then they tip up the table to an angle less than 90 degrees. For about half an hour you just stand still and everyone waits to see if you are going to have symptoms.

This is a medical story of Toby who had a condition where he fainted whenever he had eaten Nuts. After a checkup from the doctor thought he might have a condition called NOTS. Toby was certain that the condition was caused from eating nuts but the doctor wanted to run tests before coming to the conclusion, the tests was scheduled months away. Toby eventually went to a heart hospital and had a test called a turn-table test. In the test they strap you to a table, with a pillow behind your head where you lie down for a while and turn the table to an angle of more than 180 degrees. For more than half an hour you're upside-down and everyone waits to see if you are going to show the symptoms. The test confirmed the nuts were the cause of the condition.

I lost my grandmother earlier this year. She was 94 years old. She passed away on Memorial Day weekend. She had said she was ready to go, but it was still, of course, a sad moment in my life. She had gotten really frail overall and was in a nursing home the last few weeks of her life. The last time I saw her, she was asleep, and didn't wake up while I was there, but I was able to tell her that I loved her and that I hoped she had sweet dreams. It felt good to be able to do that. When we got the call, I wasn't surprised. But I still miss her, of course. She was a really interesting person. She was born to Belgian immigrants.

My grandmother died when she was almost 100 years old. She died exactly on Memorial Day weekend. She just knew it was her time to go, but I'm still sad when I think about it. She was very weak and in a nursing home. She slept through my last visit, but I still told her I really love her and wished her sweet dreams. I believe she would be happy I did that because it made me feel good. I got the call to hear she'd died and I knew it was coming. I wasn't surprised. Of course I still miss her. Her parents were from Belgium and she was a very fascinating individual to be around when she was alive.

I never knew this was even possible for me. I am still in doubt. Was this the right thing to do? Would ben be alright? I even don't know if he could take care of himself. My brain says that he could, that he is old enough to be on his own. But my heart, for some reason disagrees. He had asperger's syndrome since he was little. I always felt protective towards him. He always needed me. For everything. And i had always considered a blessing to be there for my child for even the most little of his needs. But i guess the time has come for me to let him go and make him free. To let him live his life the way he sees fit and figure out his destiny.

My child has Asperger's syndrome, his name is Ben. He is older now, and wants to become his own person and step out into adulthood. This is giving me a great deal of anxiety, because since he was a child, I have attended to the smallest of his needs. This entire process feels daunting and I am deeply afraid, however, I do feel like Ben is ready to go off on his own. I still feel very protective over my child, because I have always had to attend to his every need and protect him since he was dependant on me. But just like everyone else, he deserves to go ahead and figure out his life on his own, even if it worries me.

I guess I've been looking over my shoulder, still nervous that they might change their mind and come after me and lock me up.  It's just not like me to get in trouble with the law. The life saving measures were successful, and they were able to restore a stable pulse, after which he regained consciousness. While the medical intervention is most likely what saved his life, my mom personally believes her prayers played a role and my dad feels the same.

You lie down for a while, and then they tip up the table to an angle less than 90 degrees. For about half an hour you just stand still and everyone waits to see if you are going to have symptoms.

The story I am writing about is a medical story. For my whole life, I have had a fainting disorder. My doctor thought it might be a condition called POTS. It took months to get a cardiologist to order the test, for some reason. They seemed to test me for everything else first. I eventually went to a heart hospital and had a test called a tilt table test. In this test they strap you to a table, with a pillow behind your head. You lie down for a while, and then they tip up the table to an angle less than 90 degrees. For about half an hour you just stand still and everyone waits to see if you are going to have symptoms.

I've had a lifelong struggle with a fainting disorder, which my doctor believed could be linked to a condition called POTS. The journey to diagnosis was arduous, involving multiple tests and evaluations before finally undergoing a tilt table test at a heart hospital. This test, which lasted about half an hour, entailed being secured to a table with a pillow supporting my head, then tilted to a precise angle less than 90 degrees to monitor for symptoms. The preceding months were marked by a series of other medical tests, apparently aimed at excluding other possible causes, before arriving at this pivotal diagnostic procedure, which was a crucial step in understanding my condition.
